title: How to Protect a PDF Before Sharing It
description: A practical checklist for PDF permissions, passwords, redaction and safe sharing-plus what document protection does not guarantee.
intro: PDF protection is not one single control. Passwords, permissions, redaction and careful sharing address different risks. Choose the control that fits the information and verify the result with a trusted reader.

sections.heading: Choose a protection goal
paragraphs: A document-open password restricts opening the file, while permissions can discourage or limit actions in compatible readers. These controls do not prevent screenshots, photography or every way of copying content.
If information must not be disclosed, remove it from the document rather than relying on a visual cover or a permissions setting.

sections.heading: Redact sensitive content properly
paragraphs: Redaction should remove underlying text and related content, not merely paint a rectangle over it. After redacting, search, copy and inspect the area to make sure the sensitive text is no longer present.
Review metadata, annotations, attachments, form fields and hidden layers too. Keep an original copy in a controlled location before making changes.

sections.heading: Apply protection and test
paragraphs: Use Protect PDF to create a protected copy, or Redact PDF when removing supported content. If you need to add a signature, use Sign PDF and verify what kind of signature the tool creates.
Open the output in a compatible PDF reader and test the expected behavior. Share passwords separately through an appropriate channel, and confirm that the recipient can access the file.

faq.question: Does a PDF password make a document impossible to copy?
faq.answer: No. Protection features vary by reader and do not prevent screenshots, photography or all forms of copying.

faq.question: Is drawing a black box over text enough to redact it?
faq.answer: No. The original text may remain underneath. Use a true redaction operation and verify the output by searching and copying around the redacted area.

faq.question: Should I use a strong password?
faq.answer: If you use password protection, follow your organization’s policy and use a unique, hard-to-guess password. Deliver it separately from the document.

faq.question: Does signing a PDF mean a qualified digital signature?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. Signature types and legal effect vary. Check the tool details and applicable requirements before relying on a signature.
